projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Charlotte Burton Swope was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the World War II home front oral history of Charlotte Swope. Mrs. Swope worked in the U.S. Army depot in Columbus, Ohio, and her husband was in the U. S. Army Air Corps. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mrs. Swope's home in University Heights, Ohio, on March 27th, 2003. Charlotte was 80 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: 1941, I lived in Baltimore, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Whereabouts in Ohio is that?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: That's near Lancaster. It's about 10 miles north of Lancaster, 15 miles from Columbus.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you still in school then, or were you out of school at that point?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: In 1941, I was out of school. I was working.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you had already graduated.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I graduated in 1940.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you working?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I was working, at that time, at the Army Engineer's Depot in Columbus, Ohio. It was a Quartermaster depot also. So the Army Engineers were there and the Quartermaster. Is that what I'm thinking, Quartermaster?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I think it was supplies.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Supplies, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You took that job out of high school, then?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You had some other jobs before that?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yes. Before that, I worked for the Ohio Fuel -- Gas Company, in Newark, Ohio, and then in Baltimore, Ohio, for the same company. And then when the war broke out, I went to the Army depot.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Oh, I certainly do. I was relaxing on our sun porch with a good book and the radio on. And when it came on through the radio, of course, we all got excited. There was sort of a question in your mind. Is this true? Because we had lived through the episode with Orson Welles. And then it didn't take long that we realized that it was true.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction of the people around you to that news?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Unbelievable, I guess. As I said, at first you think, you know, it's impossible. And particularly since the Japanese people had met with the President just what -- the day before? And everything went peaceable. I don't think this small town probably was effected as much as cities were. Because I think small town people think, you know, that nothing can touch us. We're in our own little world. But it did touch us through rationing. My father was on the Ration Board.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have the sense before that that we were headed into war? Did it seem to you like the news was that there was tension that was leading us to war?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No. I think at 18 I was in my own little world. I had social interests and then my work. And as I said, with a small town you think, you know, nothing can effect you. And really, I didn't actually keep up with the world news. Because, you know, at 18 I wasn't interested. I had many other things that were far more interesting to me. So it took awhile until, of course, when they started drafting and friends that you knew were going and everything. Then it began to touch home and became more real then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You said your father worked with the Ration Board?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: He was on the Ration Board.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did he take that job right after December 7th then when they started the rationing?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I'm not sure. In Baltimore, he was -- he had meat market and grocery. So the connection with food, I think that's why he was appointed to the Ration Board, because that was just an appointment thing that you worked on. So I'm not -- I'm really not sure when they started Ration Boards.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what kind of things would he do on the Ration Board?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Oh, that's where they registered people and distributed ration books. In fact, that's where my husband, who was a teacher in the Baltimore schools -- it was called Liberty Union. And he went to the Ration Board to get his ration books and met my father. And then my father introduced us later on. So that's where we became acquainted was there in Baltimore, when he was teaching at Liberty Union. And his landlady kept telling him that she had a girl that she wanted him to meet. Well, she didn't act fast enough, because my father introduced us before.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you decide to get in there and do something for the war effort?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I can't remember whether I worked in 1941 in the fall. I guess I'd have to look in records to see when I did go to the Army depot. Everyone was trying to do what they could. And I thought it was a good opportunity, actually a good career opportunity and to get a government job was a good opportunity, too. And do something for the war effort so it all tied in and worked out fine. It was an interesting job. I was hired on as an inventory clerk, and this was for the Army Engineers. And I was assigned as an inventory clerk to the department that repaired engineering equipment, transits and all types of engineering equipment they repaired. It was a small department for the size of the depot. I think, probably, the actual repair people -- there were maybe six who did the actual repair work, six men. And then our office, there were only five in our office plus a lieutenant with the engineers. And the lady who was office manager had the black widow spiders and worked with them and asked if someone wanted to help. And I volunteered, I said sure, that sounds interesting because I knew the black widow spiders were kept there in the office. And we did, what we called, milked them. We had a room that was probably 8' by 8' square. And it was all painted white. Everything was -- well, there was nothing in the room. Except the walls were all white. And we'd take the spiders in there and let out two at a time and let them climb the walls and we collected the web on a wire frame. The reason they used the black widow spiders, it was -- they found it was the strongest and finest substance that they'd get for repairing the sights, the scopes on the engineering equipment, on the transits. And that was before nylon, or just the beginning of nylon. And eventually, the nylon killed the spiders. And we usually kept about six or eight spiders, black widows, on hand. And they came from Georgia. They were shipped in. We would order as we needed them, because their life span was not too long. We fed them. We didn't pet them. But we were humane with them, I guess that's what it is. But it was interesting because I had no idea that a black widow spider web was used for anything at all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you name them?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, we didn't name them. The turnover was too fast. And we didn't want to get too attached to them. But it was an interesting job. And she and I, I guess, we were the only two people that I know or even become acquainted with that did anything. Because this, the repair unit there was considered one of the largest -- did most of the engineering repair work for the Army. Although, as I said at the beginning, the actual, physical set up was small. But it was interesting, I liked it. It was fun.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how would they actually use the web to repair these things?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: The web was the cross bars.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The cross bar in the scopes?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: In the sights, yes. In the scopes and in the sighting material.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because it was fine and easy to --

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: It was fine and tough.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How was it attached to the scopes? Was it glued somehow or --

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I have no idea. Although, the web was a little sticky. I'm not sure that it was -- I think it was self-attaching almost, if I remember correctly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Now, that was many years ago. And the web was sticky, and I think, maybe, it was sort of self-attaching.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But it was used as the cross hairs.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: As the cross hairs in the scopes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And these were scopes that were used for non-military things, you know.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Engineers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Engineering things.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: They were used with the transits. The transits were -- you'd see the engineers out with the tripods and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: -- looking through the transits and the transits have scopes on them. So they were used principally for that. And it was interesting. I liked it. It was fun.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever get bit?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anybody in the office get bit?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No. Nobody played with them except for the office manager. Her name was Amanda Ruffner [sp]. And she, to my knowledge, was never bit. They really, I mean, you know, if you take them out on a stick and put them on the wall and let them crawl, there's no reason for them to bite you. Because if you had them on your skin and slapped at them or irritated them, that's a different thing. But we let them crawl on the walls, not on our skin. And the frames were similar to, just a rectangle frame, similar to a clothes hanger wire. It was a rectangle frame about, oh, 10" by 8", maybe. Because it had to be long enough when the web was folded so that they could work with the web between the folds. So the web that they worked with itself was not folded.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you just kind of placed this web against the frame and pulled it off or something?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yeah. You see the spiders begin to crawl up the wall and spin their web. And that's what I said, the web was sort of self-adhesive. Because you just took the end of the web and attached it to the frame. And as the spiders spin the web, you roll the frame.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you just attach the frame and let the spider do all the work.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: That's right, that's right. And I just remembered, too. In the repair shop there, they repaired -- they used mercury. And they repaired some of the engineering equipment that used mercury in -- I can't remember. I should not have started that. But I remember there was mercury there that they used. I think it was in, like the clocks where the mercury -- they put it on the numbers on the clock would shine. And shine at night that way, too. I just -- I hadn't even thought about that until now that we're speaking about it. But it was fun. It was a fun time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long would it take the spiders to give you enough web?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Oh, it depended. Because some of them, they'd crawl but they wouldn't spin, you know, they'd crawl up the wall. So you put them back in and think, well, they'll spin another day. And usually, if we were in the room a half hour, forty-five minutes with them, we'd get enough web for the repairman to use for -- depending upon -- it's hard to know how much equipment's coming in and how much you need. So sometimes, we'd be overloaded with equipment to be repaired, and we'd have to milk them more then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you basically just did it as needed.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: As needed, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't keep supplies of web.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, no. That was not a good idea. I can't remember exactly now why. But it might be the fact that it deteriorated quickly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, it deteriorated.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yeah. No, they used fresh and they liked the fresh web for the instruments. So as you said, we just did it as needed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how long did you have to do that before nylon replaced the spiders?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I don't know. I left.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, you left that job.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else that you did at that job?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I was inventory clerk.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Right.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: So I did inventory for the repair shop.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So where did you go next then?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I went to Miami Beach to be married.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay, very good. Didn't work after your marriage?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No. I did not work. I was fortunate. I traveled with my husband.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: And we saw a lot of the country. He was in the Army Air Corps in Physical Education. So we were all over the country. Saw a lot of it from coast to coast. In fact, we were married in Miami Beach on May 27th, 1943. He graduated from OCS three days later. We got on a troop train of 200 officers --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: -- and 50 wives, and went from Miami Beach, Florida, to Santa Anna, California. Since we were -- we were a troop train, but we did not have priority. It took us five days on a train because we were put on the side frequently when a troop train with priority came. But it was fun because the married couples all had their own compartments. And we were -- actually, we went from Miami Beach to Los Angeles, and that -- on the train. And then from Los Angeles down to Santa Anna where all of the officers on that troop train then had to wait for assignment to their post.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was it your impression that when you traveled the country that most people were involved in some way in the war effort or were they just going about their business? Non-military people I'm talking about.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, I think they were involved to a degree. Maybe as a civilian volunteer with the -- I'm trying to think what they call it. The civilian -- was there a Civilian Air Patrol?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Civil Defense.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Civil Defense. That's what I was trying to think of. And other volunteer groups through the Red Cross. No, I think the war touched everyone. I think everyone was involved one way or the other in it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get involved in any scrap drives or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, I didn't. Because being connected with the Air Force and we were stationed different places actually, we weren't at any one place long enough to be involved with the civilians. And there was kind of a gap between civilians and Air Corps or Army. We were accepted, but not with open arms. Because they knew we were to be at different places for a short time. And of course, if we lived on base, then you were with Army or Air Corps, or had your connection that way. Because when we were in Childress, Texas, I didn't have anything to do, so I thought it would be nice to have a job. And I quickly found out that downtown anyplace I applied, I think when I went out the door, they put the application in the trash. Because I was Army and I could understand it. They didn't know whether I'd be there six weeks or six months. And on the base, the base wasn't that large, so any of the women who were employed were non-commissioned officers' wives. So I just gave up working.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was rationing of food or shoes or whatever, was that much of a hardship?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No. Not with the Army, because we had the PX on base. And some bases -- most of the bases had the food PX, and then the regular PX where you could buy anything you wanted. So it wasn't any problem, really. Of course, the PX's did not have fresh meat. But you got that downtown. You used ration books and you learned to use it wisely. And you had one or two days a week without meat, meatless meals. So it challenged your create-ability, too. But I can't remember that it was any hardship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there ever a point, maybe earlier in the war, when the outcome was in doubt?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, I don't think so. I think everyone -- civilians and Army personnel -- everyone was every confident. But I think that's American egotism. We knew we were going to win. There wasn't any question.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was just how long?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yes. I think it probably did last longer than they had expected. But it was a good time and a bad time because we were away from family. But we started our own family while we were traveling. Yeah, we had a little girl on August 18, 1944. And it was fun. That kept me busy. I didn't need a job after we had her.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you think you got accurate accounts of the news from the news reels and from radio, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Oh, I don't think there was any question of what you did. There again, I think it was the American attitude of they're going to tell us. And of course, we got a lot of ours through the posts -- the Army posts of wherever we were stationed. So I don't remember that there was any doubt that we were getting the correct news on it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You believed what you were being told?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Well, yes. I had no reason not to believe.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you follow it pretty closely? I mean, obviously, you got your news through the Army. But do you remember going and watching news reels and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Only when we went to the movies. We were lucky because, for my husband and I, life went on pretty much as usual, except for the traveling. And we had a car and we had a plan for packing the car. Every time we moved, right down to the last pin. So it was fun. I have to say that, that it was fun. And we made good friends every place we went. And as I said, we were lucky. We had good experiences.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing any stories or reading any news or whatever about the concentration camps before they actually found the concentration camps in Germany or in Europe?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, I really don't. And the closest we came -- and not concentration camp. But at the one post when we had our transfer papers, they sent some men out from the post to make crates for our moving. And they were POW's. And I think maybe that was probably -- it brought things to reality. Because I heard them speaking German with each other. And you just don't hear that everyday. Of course, they had POW on their shirts. And I knew they were POW's because the officer that came with them, of course, assured me that it was okay because he would be there. And that they were more or less, I guess, called trustees. But I think that that was one of the things that hit home because I thought gee, these are not Americans. But they look just like we look.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were there a lot of POW's that were there working?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You don't know how many there were.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I assume you probably never had any moments when you talked to them --

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Only when they came out to our apartment and they were making crates and doing the packing for us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did the POW's seem to be happy to be over here and not fighting?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: They were doing their job. I don't know whether they were happy or not happy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You couldn't tell that from their attitude --

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, no. There didn't seem to be any bitterness, really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They were treated pretty well, I assume.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news about FDR, the day that FDR died?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yes, I do. We were living in San Antonio. And it was a beautiful day, sunny. I was -- actually, I was hanging out clothes. And I had our little girl in the walker beside me and I had the radio. So I remember that vividly. It was almost unbelievable. Because he was one of those people you thought was going on forever, you know, just like your own grandparents and parents. You think they're going to live forever. No, I remember that day very well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mostly a sad reaction from the people around you?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Shock and wondering what's going to happen now. Although we all knew that life goes on. Everybody is replaceable. So it was just more in awe and wondering what route we take now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you know anything about Truman at that point?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, I didn't. I was not a good politician.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't follow it closely, so you knew --

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, I didn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now the people around, did they know who this guy was?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The people around you. What was the general reaction to Truman taking over? Was there some doubt about his ability to finish the job?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Not to my knowledge. Not in our groups. There again, you find out that life goes on no matter what happens. Adjustments are made and it usually comes out okay in the end. I'm an optimist.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you listen to the funeral on the radio or anything? FDR's?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I don't remember that I did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They said there were news reels, but that was a few months later.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you on V-E Day?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I have to think.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That would have been early May, '45. The end of the first week in May.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I think Temple, Texas. I think that's where we were, in Temple, Texas. And my husband was at McCloskey General Hospital. It was a rehabilitation hospital. And since he was in Physical Education and had gone to get his certificate for rehabilitation. He worked out there. And they were all -- at McCloskey, most of them were amputees. But they had a basketball team with wheelchairs. They had bowling, they had golf. And I remember one man who was traveling with one arm. And he came to demonstrate that you can play golf with one arm very well. It was interesting because we had gone through Temple, Texas on a transfer and had stopped at a restaurant in Temple for lunch. And looking around, I said, oh, I think this would be so depressing because every soldier had a limb missing or a disability of some sort. And I said I hope we're never assigned here. We were assigned to Temple and I had qualms about going out to the post. And my husband kept saying, you've got to come out to the post and look around. So finally he talked me into it and I went out to the post for a Sunday. And I was shocked because it was the happiest PX that I had ever been in. The atmosphere was wonderful. And all the fellows there were so happy. And after talking with several of them, the comment was we're alive, so we're happy. We're here because we're alive. We may have some handicaps but we'll overcome them. So I had no qualms about going to the post after that, in fact, it was fun. Because it was a fun place to go. And I enjoyed watching the progress of different men in the -- just in the Physical Education part of it. Whether they were bowling or playing basketball or playing golf or whatever. It was -- it was fun to watch their progress.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any close friends or relatives during the war?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were lucky there.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, I didn't. Very lucky. And particularly coming from a small town. And my husband came from a small town, too. And I can't remember, I don't think he lost any, either, of the fellows that he grew up with or anything like that. And of course, in my small town there were some casualties, but none like in our graduating class. So we were lucky.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How was the celebration in Temple on V-E Day? Did you do anything?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You just kind of took it in stride?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: We took it in stride and well, we knew that realistically, you weren't going to be released tomorrow or next week or anything. Everything had to be cleared up. So we knew that we still had time to serve. And I think you just sort of bide your time. And Temple is a small town, too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So no wild celebrations in the street?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No wild celebration in the street that I remember. If it was, I missed it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news about the dropping of the first atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, I can't remember specifically, although I'm sure we experienced some reaction to it. But that memory is not as vivid as the others we've talked about. I hadn't thought about that. That's interesting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I guess it didn't have much of an impact on you. It just meant the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: That's true. And I think a lot of people did not know the destruction that the bomb would cause. And you knew that they were testing. And I'm not a scientist, so an atom meant nothing to me. And I think that was a lot of the reaction. Because bombs had been dropped all during the war. But there was nothing to compare, as I say, an ordinary bomb with the atom bomb. So I think it took a little while before you realized what the destruction was on that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you do any celebrating on V-J Day when the war was finally over?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No. I guess we weren't much into celebrations.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I guess not.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: I can't even remember with V-J Day where we were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That would be -- well, the bombs were dropped and they announced that there would be a surrender in August. And then the terms of the surrender were signed September 2nd of '45. So August-September, wherever you were then.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I don't remember. I'd have to look it up in my records.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you don't have the particular memories --

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No, I don't have.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- of doing anything out of the ordinary.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about World War II, being on the home front, is there any particularly vivid memory that comes to mind that you haven't talked about?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Vivid memories. My husband -- one of his favorite stories. In Childress, Texas, at the Childress Air Force Base, was Bombardier School. And the pilots had to get so many hours per month in in flying. So a lot of times, that meant they would just really go out and fly. Fly up to Oklahoma. Childress is a dry town, so they'd fly to Oklahoma to get some beer. But sometimes he would go out with one of the guys in the plane if they were doing their -- making their time for the month. There were these two brothers who were pilots, always competing. And my husband was with the one brother and the other brother and they were going out and get their time in for flying and do some -- I can't remember. I think they called it dog-fighting with the two planes like they did during World War I. So they were flying around chasing each other and the pilot that my husband was with said I'm going to lose my brother right now on our tail. I'm tired of him on our tail. And at that time, bridges spanned dry riverbeds. Because the riverbeds only had water during the wet season. But they had to have the bridges to cross the dry beds. And he flew down and went under the bridge and the brother didn't follow. So he got rid of the brother on his tail. And my husband, when he came home to tell me this story, he said that's the last time I'm flying with him. That's funny, but it's not really related to the war except pilots were young fellows. And they were sort of daredevils. And it was unusual to have two stationed at the same place -- have two brothers stationed at the same place. But they were wild ones. And I can't think of -- well, another -- I think it's funny. We were married Thursday evening at about 7:30. And there were two other couples with us. And we went -- had a little reception and had a pleasant evening. And I had gone down to Miami Beach two days before and registered at the Ronnie [sp] Plaza as Miss, because I was not married then. So we had the little party. And the two other couples -- it was not wife privilege night, which in OCS -- that's the only time that you can stay with your wife was on wife privilege night. So they took their wives back to their rooms. And my husband and I went to the Ronnie Plaza where I was registered. And he was going to take me up to the room. The lady on the desk was about 60 years old. And she yelled across the lobby, where are you going? And my husband said, I'm taking my wife up to her room. And she said, no, you're not. You're not going to get on that elevator because she's registered as Miss. And he said but look, we have our wedding rings. She has her corsage, we just got married. The lady said, where's the certificate. And my husband said, well, the chaplain has it to be signed. She said you're not taking your wife any place, if that is your wife. So he went back to his hotel and I went, on my wedding night, to my room and washed my hair. So that was my wedding night. But there are funny things that happened. We had fun.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you -- go ahead. Do you have something else?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you think the entertainment industry, movies, radio, did a good job of keeping morale up?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yes, I think so. And when you said about the movies, Clark Gable's class, my husband went in just as Clark Gable was leaving at Miami Beach. And in my husband's class, old people probably remember him. Oh, that's been on, I bet. John Carroll, a movie star, was in my husband's class. And he was a nice -- handsome. Beautiful, beautiful voice. And he sang at commencement. He sang The Lord's Prayer. I don't know what's happened to him since then. He did some movies after the war, I know. But I don't know -- I've often wondered what happened to him because it seems as if -- at that time, that he had a promising career. But no, I think the movie people -- I think they did their share, because there were many of them that were in the service. And Clark Gable, actually, he was old enough that he could've gotten out of it, because he was one of the older fellows in OCS. And there were a lot of them as you think about it, in the service. James Stewart, I don't know whether Henry Fonda was or not. I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't remember hearing anything about him.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: But there were a lot of them. They did their share through the bond drives and all, too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever go to any war bond rallies or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Never went to one.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Never went to one. Did you buy war bonds?

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: Yes. Yes, we bought them. And then spent them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Cashed them in and spent the money.

sp.speaker: Charlotte Burton Swope
sp.p: But it was nice to have when we came home, though. Oh, I think everybody bought war bonds even after the war. Yeah, even after the war there was some campaigns on to continue with automatic withdraw from pay checks. No, I think the American people -- we always rally up to the cause. And so far we've come through very well, very well.
